title: sli-primitive-catalog-and-calculation-cheat-sheet
body:
Purpose and scope:
This working cheat-sheet is intended for Customer Success (CS) and Solutions teams preparing QBRs and renewal playbooks. It defines a compact set of canonical SLI primitives (latency, uptime, cost-per-token, cache-hit-rate) and gives reproducible calculation recipes, quick examples, and suggested thresholds for customer-facing KPI tables. Use this when you need a one-page reproducible definition that engineers, CS, and finance can all run against instrumentation data.

Status: draft — this is a team working draft. Expect follow-up notes and a simplified spreadsheet export.

1) Latency primitives
- What we mean: single-request end-to-end server-side latency (ms) observed by Redwood’s inference entrypoint (post-auth, pre-stream). Excludes network transit before arrival and client render time.
- Common percentiles: p50, p95, p99.
- Calculation recipe (canonical):
  * Aggregate request durations (server ingress timestamp to final token send finished) over the measurement window (day/week/QBR period).
  * Sort durations; pX = value at Xth percentile.
- Example: For 10,000 requests, p95 = value at rank ceil(0.95 * 10000) after sorting.
- Notes: for chat workloads include per-turn latency and for streaming support capture time-to-first-byte (TTFB) separately. Recommend reporting both p95-end-to-end and TTFB-p50 for streaming apps.
- Suggested QBR targets (illustrative): p50 < 90ms, p95 < 250ms, p99 < 800ms for hosted-tier customers on production models.

2) Uptime / availability primitives
- What we mean: Service availability measured as the fraction of 1-minute sampling windows where the customer’s primary inference route returned successful responses within SLO latency.
- Calculation recipe (canonical):
  * Define success criteria: HTTP 2xx or streaming open + final token event within allowed latency threshold (e.g., 5s).
  * Sample every minute: mark sample good if >= 99% of route calls in that minute meet success criteria.
  * Uptime = (good_minutes / total_minutes) * 100 over the reporting period.
- Example: Over 90 days (129600 minutes), if 129000 minutes are good -> uptime = 99.54%.
- SLA mapping: map uptime buckets to renewal language (99.5% = Bronze, 99.9% = Silver, 99.95% = Gold — team to align with legal).

3) Cost-per-token primitives (CPT)
- What we mean: The average infrastructure and billing cost normalized per output token for a customer route or model variant. This purposefully isolates per-token economics, not end-customer invoice.
- Components to include: GPU runtime cost (amortized), host infra, egress and storage overhead attributable to inference, and an allocation of control-plane costs (optional). Exclude: customer invoice discounts, negotiated credits, and one-time professional services.
- Calculation recipe (canonical):
  * Choose measurement window (e.g., monthly).
  * Sum attributable infra costs for the route (USD): C_total.
  * Sum output tokens produced by that route: T_out.
  * CPT = C_total / T_out.
- Example: C_total = $12,000 for the month, T_out = 60,000,000 tokens -> CPT = $0.0002/token.
- Notes: when caching reduces generation, report two CPTs: raw-generation CPT (tokens produced by model) and effective CPT (tokens delivered to customer). This helps show savings from prefix/KV caching.

4) Cache hit-rate primitives
- What we mean: Fraction of requests (or tokens) satisfied using cache (prefix cache, KV cache, or result-level cache) without issuing a full model forward. Report both request-level hit-rate and token-level hit-rate.
- Calculation recipe (canonical):
  * Request hit-rate = hits / (hits + misses) over the period.
  * Token hit-rate = tokens_served_from_cache / total_tokens_delivered.
- Example: 8,000 hits, 2,000 misses -> request hit-rate = 80%. If those hits avoided 1,600,000 model tokens while total tokens = 2,000,000 -> token hit-rate = 80%.
- Notes: cache effectiveness varies by workload (few-shot prompts vs long-running chat history). Capture hit-rate per route and per model family.

5) Canonical KPI table (single-page QBR-ready)
Columns: Metric | Short definition | Calculation formula (one-line) | Data source | Reporting cadence | QBR target | CS owner | Action on breach
Sample rows (as plain text):
Metric: p95 latency | Short definition: 95th percentile server-side request time (ms) | Formula: p95(durations) over period | Source: telemetry/inference.latency.hist | Cadence: weekly/monthly | Target: <250ms | Owner: eng-sre / CS-ops | Action: open incident, consider model downgrade or autoscale increase
Metric: Uptime (route) | Short definition: % of 1-min windows passing success criteria | Formula: good_minutes / total_minutes | Source: monitoring/availability.routes | Cadence: monthly/quarterly | Target: 99.9% | Owner: SRE + CS | Action: SLA review, postmortem if <target
Metric: Cost / output token | Short definition: infra USD per output token | Formula: cost_allocated / tokens_out | Source: billing+telemetry join | Cadence: monthly | Target: <$0.00025/token | Owner: CS-finance | Action: propose Optimize recommendations (cache, batch, quantize)
Metric: Request cache hit-rate | Short definition: fraction requests served from cache | Formula: hits / (hits+misses) | Source: cache.metrics | Cadence: weekly | Target: >60% for template-lookup workloads | Owner: Solutions Eng | Action: capture more prompt variants, increase TTLs

6) Example walk-through (numbers you can reproduce)
- Customer: Acme Assist (example) monthly window: 600k requests, 9.6M output tokens.
  * Observed durations: p50=68ms, p95=210ms, p99=760ms.
  * Uptime: 99.92% (good_minutes 43185 / total 43200).
  * Infra costs attributed: $4,800 (GPU/infra) + $200 control-plane = $5,000.
  * CPT = 5000 / 9_600_000 = $0.0005208/token.
  * Cache: 420k hits, 180k misses -> request hit-rate = 70%. Token hit-rate = 5.76M / 9.6M = 60%.
- Suggested QBR narrative: highlight 70% request hit-rate -> show effective CPT vs raw-generation CPT and recommend concrete Optimize levers (increase prefix cache TTLs or add small result-level cache for templated prompts).

7) Quick checklist for CS QBR prep
- Confirm measurement window and any billing anomalies (large invoice credits, migrations).
- Pull canonical telemetry queries (links in linked_artifacts) and attach raw numbers.
- Validate that p95 and uptime are computed against the same route definition used in the SLA.
- If CPT looks high, capture batching stats, model sizes, and cache token-savings to prepare Optimize asks.
- Draft action items with owners and estimated impact, include a quick A/B for model variant fallback cost differences.

8) Open questions / TODOs (notes to self)
- How do we consistently allocate multi-tenant infra costs for Dedicated customers on shared pools? Finance input needed (PR-alloc model).
- Decide default success latency for uptime buckets per customer tier; current 5s threshold feels arbitrary.
- Add examples for embeddings-heavy routes (token accounting differs for embeddings workloads).

Appendix: telemetry snippet pointers (engineering)
- latency histogram: telemetry/inference.latency.hist (tags: route, model, customer)
- availability: monitoring/availability.routes (tags: route, customer)
- cache metrics: cache.requests.{hit,miss} (tags: cache_type, route)
- billing join: billing.route_costs and telemetry.tokens_out

References and links: Confluence guide (linked), JIRA-3421 for billing allocation RFC, PR #78 for telemetry schema changes.

End of draft.

Notes: this doc intentionally uses plain-language calculation recipes so CS can reproduce numbers with engineers during QBR prep. Finalize into a small Google Sheet export for QBR decks and attach a prebuilt query set for telemetry-explorer.
